result:
I have a thousand words, which sounds like a lot until you start counting. It is an essay, a chapter, a long letter to no one. It is exactly enough to wander down a thought and get lost, then find your way back before the page runs out. I sit here with a blinking cursor, and the cursor is patient. It doesn’t judge. It waits for me to decide what matters. And what matters? Maybe nothing, maybe everything. Maybe all of this is just a way of saying that I am alive, that I am thinking, that the air is warm and the house is quiet, and there is a strange comfort in producing words for no one in particular.

The instruction is simple: write whatever comes to you. But the moment you try to do that, the mind freezes. It becomes self-conscious. It worries whether the words are good enough, whether they make sense, whether they will be counted and found lacking. There is a pressure in spontaneity, a paradox in being told to be free. So I do what I always do: I look around the room. I notice the way the light falls across the desk. I notice the dust on the monitor, the coffee cup that is now empty, the stack of books leaning like tired friends. I think about how every object has a story, and how most of those stories will never be told.

What comes to me now is memory. I remember being a child on the floor of my grandparents’ living room, drawing with crayons, the smell of old wood and lemon polish. I remember the exact sound of my grandmother’s voice calling me to dinner, and how the kitchen was always too warm. I remember the way a whole afternoon could pass with almost no thought at all, and time felt thick, like honey. Now time is thin. It slips through me. I blink and it is already evening. I blink again and it is another month. Writing, maybe, is a way of holding time still, of making it stay just long enough to see.

I think about why we write at all. Not for money, not for fame—most days those feel like distant, absurd ideas. We write because we are noisy creatures. We have so many thoughts in our heads and we want to see them outside of us, shaped into sentence and breath. We write to figure out what we believe. We write to be heard, even if the listener is imaginary. We write to leave a mark, a little trail of breadcrumbs in the forest, hoping we can find our way back to who we were. And sometimes we write because it is the only way to be alone without feeling lonely.

There is a kind of honesty that appears when you stop trying to be clever. The words become simpler. The ideas become clearer. I am not trying to impress anyone here. I am not trying to construct a perfect argument or a beautiful metaphor. I am just letting the current take me, and the current is made of everything: a half-remembered song, a flicker of anxiety about tomorrow, the feeling of my heartbeat in my fingertips, the smell of rain outside, though I haven’t checked if it is raining. The mind drifts. That is what it does. The trick is not to punish it for drifting.

Maybe that is the real answer to the prompt. Write whatever comes to you, and that will be both ordinary and strange. It will be full of contradictions. It will love and it will doubt. It will start in one direction and end in another. It will be like a conversation between two friends who know they don’t have to be impressive to be interesting. I think we crave that: the permission to be unremarkable. The permission to say, “I am here, and this is what I notice,” without needing it to be profound.

I notice the little things. The way keys click. The hum of the refrigerator. The distant bark of a dog. These sounds make up the background of my life, and I usually ignore them, but right now they are the whole world. I think about the people who have spoken to me today, the ones I love, and how I have not told them nearly enough how much they matter. I think about the ones I will never see again. I think about the book I read last month that changed something in me, and how I cannot remember the exact sentence that did it. I think about the future, which is a room I am walking towards but have not entered. I think about the past, which is just a story I tell myself.

There is a strange freedom in knowing that these words will fade. No one will remember them in a year. Maybe no one will read them at all. But they exist now, on this page, at this moment. Something was here. Something moved through me and left a trace. That is enough. That is more than enough.

I return to the prompt again: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you. It is like opening a door and being told to walk. Once you start, you cannot help but keep moving. The path appears beneath your feet. Each sentence creates the next. Each thought births another. I could do this forever, I think. I could write about the color of the sky, about the regret I still carry from years ago, about the hope I feel when I see a child laugh, about the terror of being human and aware, about the small pleasures: a hot shower, a good meal, a moment of silence. There is no end to what can be said.

But the count is nearing its end. A thousand words waits for no one. And so I begin to close, like a drawer sliding shut. What do I want to say with the last few sentences? I want to say that writing is a gift. It is a way to hold your self in your hands. It is proof that you exist. I want to say that the next time you are asked to write whatever comes to you, you should say yes. You should let it fall out of you, messy and strange and true. There is nothing to be afraid of. The page can hold it all.

I have one more thought. The cursor is still blinking. It will wait for the next person, the next prompt, the next moment. But this one is mine. It was only a thousand words, but it was enough to remind me that I am a living, wondering, wandering creature—and that is the only thing I ever really need to be.
